content: Erythromycin base interacts with various drugs by influencing their metabolism, transport, or pharmacodynamic effects. Below are the detailed interactions and recommendations for monitoring or adjusting therapy: 1. Deflazacort: Erythromycin increases deflazacort levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Monitor therapy closely and consider dose adjustments. 2. Deutetrabenazine: Both drugs increase the QTc interval. While deutetrabenazine does not prolong QTc to a clinically significant extent at maximum doses, caution is advised due to potential risks of torsades de pointes or sudden death under certain conditions (e.g., bradycardia, hypokalemia, or co-administration with other QT-prolonging drugs). 3. Dexamethasone: Erythromycin increases dexamethasone levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 4. Diazepam (buccal and intranasal): Erythromycin increases diazepam levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors may reduce diazepam elimination, increasing the risk of adverse effects. Monitor therapy closely. 5. Dienogest/Estradiol Valerate: Erythromycin increases levels of these hormones by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism but may decrease their levels by altering intestinal flora. This applies only to oral forms, with a low risk of contraceptive failure. Consider additional birth control methods during co-administration. 6. Digoxin: Erythromycin increases digoxin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 7. Disopyramide: Erythromycin increases disopyramide levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 8. Docetaxel: Erythromycin increases docetaxel levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein efflux. Monitor therapy closely. 9. Dolasetron: Both drugs increase the QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely and consider modifying treatment. 10. Donepezil: Erythromycin increases donepezil levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 11. Doxorubicin (including liposomal formulations): Erythromycin increases doxorubicin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein efflux. Monitor therapy closely. 12. Dutasteride: Erythromycin increases dutasteride levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 13. Duvelisib: Duvelisib increases erythromycin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, and erythromycin increases duvelisib levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely and adjust doses as needed. 14. Efavirenz: Erythromycin increases efavirenz levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 15. Elagolix: Elagolix increases erythromycin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition and decreases them by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely and consider dose adjustments for CYP3A substrates. 16. Eliglustat: Eliglustat increases erythromycin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely and adjust dosages as needed. 17. Eluxadoline: Eluxadoline increases erythromycin levels by reducing metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 18. Elvitegravir/Cobicistat/Emtricitabine/Tenofovir DF: This combination increases erythromycin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Cobicistat is contraindicated with CYP3A4 substrates that have a narrow therapeutic index. Monitor therapy closely. 19. Encorafenib: Encorafenib both inhibits and induces CYP3A4, increasing erythromycin levels. 20. Eplerenone: Erythromycin increases eplerenone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 21. Erlotinib: Erythromycin increases erlotinib levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 22. Estradiol: Erythromycin decreases estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora but increases levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. This applies only to oral forms, with a low risk of contraceptive failure. Monitor therapy closely. 23. Estrogens (conjugated synthetic and esterified): Erythromycin decreases levels by altering intestinal flora but increases levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. This applies only to oral forms, with a low risk of contraceptive failure. Monitor therapy closely. 24. Estropipate: Erythromycin decreases estropipate levels by altering intestinal flora but increases levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. This applies only to oral forms, with a low risk of contraceptive failure. Monitor therapy closely. 25. Eszopiclone: Erythromycin increases eszopiclone levels by enhancing gastrointestinal absorption and inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Reduce the starting dose of eszopiclone to 1 mg/day and monitor therapy closely. 26. Ethinylestradiol: Erythromycin decreases ethinylestradiol levels by altering intestinal flora, with a low risk of contraceptive failure. Antibiotics may reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Monitor therapy closely. 27. Etoposide: Erythromycin increases etoposide levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein efflux. Monitor therapy closely. 28. Eucalyptus: Erythromycin increases eucalyptus levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 29. Exemestane: Erythromycin increases exemestane levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 30. Ezogabine: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor QT interval closely, especially at higher ezogabine doses. 31. Fedratinib: Fedratinib increases erythromycin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Adjust doses of CYP3A4 substrates as necessary and monitor therapy closely. 32. Finasteride: Erythromycin increases finasteride levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 33. Finererone: Erythromycin increases finererone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor serum potassium during initiation and dosage adjustments. 34. Flecainide: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 35. Fludrocortisone: Erythromycin increases fludrocortisone levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 36. Fluoxetine: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 37. Fluvastatin: Erythromycin increases fluvastatin toxicity by inhibiting OATP1B1 transporters, increasing the risk of myopathy. Monitor therapy closely. 38. Fluvoxamine: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 39. Foscarnet: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 40. Fostamatinib: Fostamatinib increases erythromycin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor for toxicities and adjust dosages as needed. 41. Fostemsavir: Fostemsavir increases erythromycin levels by inhibiting OATP1B1/3 transporters. Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 42. Gadobenate: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 43. Gemtuzumab: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 44. Gentamicin: Erythromycin increases gentamicin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 45. Gepirone: Erythromycin increases gepirone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 46. Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir: Erythromycin increases levels of this combination via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 47. Goserelin: Goserelin increases erythromycin toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Monitor therapy closely. 48. Guanfacine: Erythromycin increases guanfacine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Reduce guanfacine dosage to half the recommended dose for extended-release formulations. 49. Histrelin: Histrelin increases erythromycin toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Monitor therapy closely. 50. Hydrocortisone: Erythromycin increases hydrocortisone levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 51. Hydroxyzine: Hydroxyzine increases erythromycin toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Monitor therapy closely. 52. Ibrutinib: Erythromycin increases ibrutinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Reduce ibrutinib dose to 280 mg/day for B-cell malignancies or 420 mg/day for graft-versus-host disease when co-administered with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors. 53. Ifosfamide: Erythromycin decreases ifosfamide levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing therapeutic effects. Monitor therapy closely. 54. Iloperidone: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Iloperidone increases erythromycin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 55. Imatinib: Erythromycin increases imatinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein efflux. Monitor therapy closely. 56. Indacaterol (inhaled): Erythromycin increases indacaterol levels by modulating P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4 activity. No dose adjustment is needed at the 75 mcg dose. Monitor therapy closely. 57. Indinavir: Erythromycin increases indinavir levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 58. Insulin (various formulations): Erythromycin and insulin may synergistically lower blood glucose levels. Monitor therapy closely. 59. Irinotecan (including liposomal formulations): Erythromycin increases irinotecan levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 60. Isavuconazonium sulfate: Erythromycin increases isavuconazonium levels by inhibiting CYP2E1 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 61. Isradipine: Erythromycin increases isradipine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 62. Istradefylline: Istradefylline increases erythromycin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein efflux. Monitor therapy closely. 63. Itraconazole: Erythromycin increases itraconazole levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein efflux. Monitor therapy closely. 64. Ivacaftor: Erythromycin increases ivacaftor levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Reduce ivacaftor dose when co-administered with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors. 65. Ivermectin: Erythromycin increases ivermectin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 66. Ivosidenib: Erythromycin increases ivosidenib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, increasing the risk of QTc prolongation. Monitor therapy closely. 67. Ketoconazole: Erythromycin and ketoconazole increase each other's levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 68. Lapatinib: Erythromycin increases lapatinib levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 69. Larotrectinib: Erythromycin increases larotrectinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 70. Lenacapavir: Lenacapavir increases erythromycin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 71. Lenvatinib: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor ECG closely when co-administered. 72. Letermovir: Letermovir increases erythromycin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 73. Leuprolide: Leuprolide increases erythromycin toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Monitor therapy closely. 74. Levamlodipine: Erythromycin increases levamlodipine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor for symptoms of hypotension and edema. 75. Levofloxacin: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 76. Levoketoconazole: Erythromycin and levoketoconazole increase each other's levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 77. Levonorgestrel/Ethinylestradiol/Ferrous Bisglycinate: Erythromycin decreases hormone levels by altering intestinal flora, with a low risk of contraceptive failure. Monitor therapy closely. 78. Lomitapide: Lomitapide increases erythromycin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Consider dose reduction when co-administered. 79. Loperamide: Erythromycin increases loperamide levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 80. Lorlatinib: Lorlatinib decreases erythromycin levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 81. Lumateperone: Erythromycin increases lumateperone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Reduce lumateperone dose to 21 mg/day when co-administered. 82. Lurasidone: Erythromycin increases lurasidone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Reduce starting dose to 20 mg/day and maximum dose to 80 mg/day. 83. Maraviroc: Erythromycin increases maraviroc levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 84. Mavacamten: Erythromycin increases mavacamten levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Reduce mavacamten dose when co-administered. 85. Mavorixafor: Erythromycin increases mavorixafor levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein efflux. Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 86. Mefloquine: Erythromycin increases mefloquine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 87. Mestranol: Erythromycin decreases mestranol levels by altering intestinal flora but increases levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 88. Methadone: Both drugs increase QTc interval. Monitor therapy closely. 89. Methylprednisolone: Erythromycin increases methylprednisolone levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 90. Mifepristone: Erythromycin increases mifepristone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Both drugs increase QTc interval. Use alternatives if available. 91. Mipomersen: Both drugs may increase hepatic enzyme levels. Monitor liver function tests (LFTs) closely. 92. Mitotane: Mitotane decreases erythromycin levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 93. Mitoxantrone: Erythromycin increases mitoxantrone levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition. Monitor therapy closely. 94. Momelotinib: Erythromycin increases momelotinib toxicity by inhibiting OATP1B1/B3 transporters. Monitor therapy closely. 95. Montelukast: Erythromycin increases montelukast levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely. 96. Naldemedine: Erythromycin increases naldemedine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor therapy closely.
